description: Jejuri, in Purandar taluka of Pune district about 50 km from the city, is the principal centre of worship of Khandoba, also known as Malhari Martand and regarded as a form of Shiva. He is the family deity of many Maharashtrian communities. The temple crowns a hill and is laid out like a small fort, with a walled courtyard and an approach stairway lined with stone lamp pillars. During festivals devotees throw turmeric over the steps and surroundings, which gives the place its nickname Sonyachi Jejuri, or Golden Jejuri. One bell in the temple is described as a trophy from the Maratha victory over the Portuguese at Vasai, attributed to Chimaji Appa. Management lies with the Shree Martand Dev Sansthan trust.

description: The Dilwara temples stand in a forested hill range about 2.5 km from Mount Abu in Sirohi district, Rajasthan, and belong to the Svetambara Jain tradition. According to Wikipedia, five temples sit inside one walled compound, dedicated to Rishabhanatha, Neminatha, Parshvanatha and Mahavira, and they are counted among the five great tirthas of the Svetambara sect. They are built of white marble in the Solanki (Maru-Gurjara) style and are noted for fine carving, especially in Vimal Vasahi and Luna Vasahi, where the latter has a central dome with rings of tirthankara and monk figures. The temples are administered from Sirohi by the Seth Shri Kalyanji Parmanandji Pedhi, which also runs a nearby dining hall (bhojanshala).

description: Tanot Mata temple lies in Jaisalmer district in western Rajasthan, roughly 122 km from Jaisalmer city and close to the Pakistan border. According to Wikipedia, the goddess is Tanot Mata, identified with Aavad, a daughter of Mamadia Charan and regarded in Charan literature as an incarnation of Hinglaj Mata. According to Wikipedia, tradition holds that the Bhati king Tanu Rao installed the idol in 828 AD. The temple is best known for local accounts that most of about 3,000 shells fired toward it in the 1965 war missed or failed to explode; the Border Security Force reportedly took over its management afterwards. A victory tower (Vijay Stambha), built by the Indian Army after 1971 to commemorate the Battle of Longewala, stands in the compound.

description: Nakodaji is a Shvetambara Jain pilgrimage site in the Mewanagar (Balotra) area of western Rajasthan, historically part of Barmer district, between the villages of Vikrampura and Nakoda. Its central image is Parshvanatha, a 24-inch black stone idol, and the complex also enshrines Nakoda Bhairava, a guardian deity revered by both Jains and Hindus. According to Wikipedia, Jain legend credits Acharya Sthulabhadra with the original shrine, the present structure dates to the Solanki era, and the main image was reinstalled in 1449 after being hidden from an invader. The marble and sandstone temple has many small domed sub-shrines, a basement chamber of idols, and a dharamshala for pilgrims and a community dining hall. description: The Palitana temples crown the Shatrunjaya hills, about 2 km south of Palitana town in Bhavnagar district, Gujarat. They belong to the Shvetambara Murtipujaka tradition of Jainism and form one of its most important pilgrimage sites. Wikipedia describes roughly 900 shrines and larger temples grouped in fortified enclosures called tuks along the ridges, with the principal temple dedicated to Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara. Jain tradition links the hill to remote antiquity, though Wikipedia says the surviving temples date from about the 11th century onward. Pilgrims climb roughly 3,500 stone steps from the town, and sources say no one stays overnight on the hill and the temples close in the monsoon. The Anandji Kalyanji Trust is reported to manage them.

description: Morgaon, a village on the Karha river in Baramati taluka of Pune district, is home to the Mayureshwar (Moreshwar) temple, a Ganesha shrine regarded as the starting and ending point of the Ashtavinayak circuit. description: The Ambreshwar Shiva Temple, also called Shiv Mandir or Puratana Shivalaya, stands on the bank of the Waldhuni river in Ambarnath, Thane district, about 2 km from Ambarnath railway station (east). It is a basalt temple in the bhumija style, dated to about 1060 AD (an inscription there is reported to record work of that year), and attributed to the Shilahara dynasty: king Chhittaraja is thought to have built it and his son Mummuni to have renovated or rebuilt it. It is a centrally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India. Its distinctive feature is a sanctum set below the level of the hall, reached by roughly twenty steps and open to the sky. The tower is missing above the hall roof; accounts differ on whether it was never completed or was later lost. The three-porched hall retains damaged carvings of divine and female figures. Shiva is the deity, and Maha Shivratri draws large crowds, with a fair held around the festival.

description: ISKCON Juhu, also known as Hare Krishna Land, is a Krishna temple complex near Juhu beach in Mumbai. Its principal deities are Sri Sri Radha Rasabihari, Sri Sri Gaura-Nitai and Sri Sri Sita Rama Laxman Hanuman, which the temple says A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada installed himself. The site says Prabhupada acquired the land in the early 1970s, when the area was remote, and that the Radha Rasabihari deities were first kept in a modest shed before the complex opened in 1978. The four-acre grounds have a marble temple, an auditorium, a restaurant and a guest house. The temple's website also hosts daily darshan and live-stream pages, and offers donation and seva options.

description: Kasba Ganpati is a Ganesh temple in Kasba Peth, the old core of Pune, regarded as the city's gramdevata, or village deity. According to Wikipedia and a Free Press Journal feature, tradition holds that a self-manifested Ganesh image was found in Pune in the 1630s and that Jijabai had the temple built. The Free Press Journal adds that the temple was built in the Pune wada style and that the Peshwas later added wooden work. The deity is honoured as Pune's first Manacha (most revered) Ganpati, and its mandal leads the final-day immersion procession of the public Ganesh festival. Wikipedia names Shri Kasba Ganpati Mandal as the group that celebrated the festival at the temple, and the Free Press Journal quotes a treasurer of the Kasba Ganpati Trust.

description: The Mumbadevi Temple stands in the Bhuleshwar and Zaveri Bazaar area of South Mumbai, set among busy markets. It is dedicated to the goddess Mumba, described by Wikipedia as a local form of Parvati (the trust calls her Shakti) and honoured as a guardian of the Koli fishing community; a popular etymology links the name of Mumbai to her. The temple trust says the present shrine dates from the 18th century and was first built at Bori Bunder before being rebuilt at Zaveri Bazaar, while Wikipedia gives conflicting dates. Wikipedia describes a black stone image of the goddess with a silver crown, with Annapurna and a tiger vahana nearby. The trust site also lists shrines of Jagadamba, Annapurna and Hanuman, and says it is managed by Shree Mumbadevi Mandir Charities, a registered public charitable trust.

description: Pataleshwar is a rock-cut Shiva temple on Jangali Maharaj Road in Shivajinagar, Pune, carved out of rock. Wikipedia assigns it to the Rashtrakuta period, around the 8th century CE, and notes that it was recorded in 19th-century surveys under names such as Bhamburda and Panchaleshvara. The cave lies below the level of the present road, and a courtyard there holds a circular Nandi pavilion, which originally had sixteen pillars, some now lost, in front of the main cave. The hall has a pillared porch and three sanctums, now with Shiva, Parvati and Ganesha, and a passage circles them. Parts look unfinished. Wikipedia says it is a protected monument looked after by the Archaeological Survey of India, and a heritage page says entry is free (check current ASI rules before visiting).

description: The Shitaladevi Temple is in Mahim, in western Mumbai, at the junction of Lady Jamshedji Road and Sitaladevi Temple Road. It honours Sitala, the goddess linked in Hindu tradition with fevers, rashes and smallpox, and described in the Sitala Mahatmya as a cooling, healing figure carrying a broom, a winnow and a pot of water. A Vithoba and Rakhumai shrine stands in front, with the goddess behind it, and the compound also has a shrine to Shantadurga. The temple's origins are unclear. One writer speculates that Raja Bimbadev brought the goddess to Mahim from Kelwe in the 13th century, but admits there is no firm evidence. A Mumbai Metro Line 3 station nearby is named after the temple.

description: The Chaturshringi Temple stands on a hill slope along Senapati Bapat Road in Pune. Its presiding goddess is Chaturshringi, also called Ambareshwari, and Wikipedia says she is regarded as the city's presiding deity, with Durga and Ganesha shrines and miniature Ashtavinayaka figures in the complex. According to Wikipedia, a legend credits a merchant devotee of the goddess Saptashrungi of Vani with finding a self-formed image of the goddess here after she appeared in a dream. The temple is said to date to the time of Shivaji. Reaching the goddess means climbing over two hundred steps, and the Incredible India tourism page notes fountains, a waterfall and pilgrim lodgings on the premises. A fair is held at the foot of the hill around Navratri.

description: The Jivdani Mata Temple crowns a hill in eastern Virar, on the northern edge of the Mumbai region in Palghar district. The goddess Jivdani is described by Wikipedia as an avatar of Mahadevi. According to the legend it records, the Pandavas worshipped here during their exile and a herdsman later found the goddess by following a cow up the hill; the original sanctum is a hollow in a cave niche, while the present marble image is a recent installation. Devotees climb a long flight of steps, about 1,465 per Wikipedia and 1,375 per the Palghar district site, and a hilltop fort and a Krishna shrine are nearby. Crowds gather on Sundays and during Navratri, and a fair is held at Dussehra.

description: The Prabhadevi temple stands in the Prabhadevi neighbourhood of Mumbai, near Dadar. It is a Devi temple and is separate from the Shree Siddhivinayak Ganapati temple, which is also in this locality. The deity is Prabhavati Devi, earlier known as Shakambari Devi. According to Wikipedia, the main idol dates to the 12th century while the present temple was raised in 1715. Folklore holds that the goddess appeared in a dream to Shyam Nayak, a Pathare Prabhu devotee, who then built the shrine. The Pathare Prabhu community site adds that the idols were moved to safer places to escape vandalism during the Mughal period and that a trust formed by Nayak's descendants, the Kirtikar family, manages the temple. An annual ten-day festival is held in the month of Paush, beginning on Shakhambari Purnima.

description: Sarasbaug Ganpati, formally the Shree Siddhivinayak temple, lies in Pune near the foot of Parvati hill. Wikipedia explains that after the Devdeveshwar temple on Parvati hill was completed, Balaji Baji Rao (Nanasaheb Peshwa) developed the surroundings in the 18th century and had a lake built at its base with a small island in the middle. The island was later turned into a garden that Nanasaheb Peshwa named Sarasbaug. According to the same source, Sawai Madhavrao Peshwa built a small temple on the island in 1784 and installed an idol of Siddhivinayak Gajanan, a form of Ganesha. The shrine therefore sits within a garden set in a lake, and it draws large crowds on Ganesh Chaturthi. Wikipedia does not say who manages the temple.

description: Shree Vajreshwari Yogini Devi temple is in the village of Vajreshwari (also called Vajrabai), in Bhiwandi taluka of Thane district, near the Tansa river and roughly 75 km from Mumbai. Outlook Traveller recounts the local tradition that Chimaji Appa, before attacking the Portuguese-held Vasai Fort, prayed to the goddess and vowed to build a grand temple if he won. The shrine is reached by a steep climb. The area is also known for its hot springs, including the Akloli Kund about a kilometre away, reputed locally to have curative properties.

description: Siddhivinayak at Siddhatek is the second shrine in the prescribed Ashtavinayak circuit, set on a hillock on the northern bank of the Bhima river in Karjat taluka of Ahmednagar district (now also called Ahilyanagar). The deity is a self-manifested Ganesha image whose trunk turns to the right, which Wikipedia describes as unique among the eight shrines; the temple site describes it as roughly three feet tall, facing north, with Riddhi and Siddhi on one lap. According to tradition recounted on the trust's site, Vishnu worshipped Ganesha here before defeating the demons Madhu and Kaitabha and attained siddhi, giving the place its name. Wikipedia credits the present temple to Ahilyabai Holkar and says the Chinchwad Devasthan Trust manages it. Devotees often walk circuits around the hill.

description: Walkeshwar Temple and the Banganga Tank lie together on Malabar Hill in South Mumbai, a few dozen metres from the sea. The temple is dedicated to Shiva. Wikipedia says it was built in 1127 by Lakshman Prabhu, a minister of the Silhara kings, damaged by the Portuguese in the 16th century and rebuilt in 1715 by the Gaud Saraswat merchant Rama Kamat, who also funded work on the tank. According to legend, Rama made a sand lingam here, and his brother Lakshmana shot an arrow into the ground to bring forth water while they searched for Sita; the tank's name means Ganga from an arrow. The Gaud Saraswat Temple Trust owns the complex, and the tank is the setting for lamp-lighting at Dev Diwali.

description: Tulshibaug Ram Mandir stands in the Tulshibaug market precinct of Pune's old city, Maharashtra, and is dedicated to Lord Ram. According to Wikipedia, the sanctum holds images of Ram, Sita and Lakshmana, with Hanuman and Ganapati-Parvati also installed, and the precinct includes smaller shrines to Ganesh, Vitthal-Rukmini, Dattatreya and Shiva. Wikipedia says it was commissioned in the Peshwa era by Naro Appaji Khire, a Pune subedar, and that it is managed by Shree Ramji Sansthan. Atlas Obscura notes that the site takes its name from a tulsi garden that once stood here, and describes a tall spire, a nagarkhana (drum house) over the northern gateway and wall murals. Wikipedia mentions a restoration project begun in 2009.

description: Swaminarayan Akshardham is a large mandir complex in Sector 20 of Gandhinagar, Gujarat, built by the Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS). Its official site describes it as a tribute to Bhagwan Swaminarayan and to the avatars, devas and sages of Hinduism, and says the carved sandstone mandir holds over 200 murtis. According to the same site it opened on 30 October 1992, was inspired by Yogiji Maharaj and was created under Pramukh Swami Maharaj. Besides the mandir, the campus has exhibitions, an Abhishek Mandapam where visitors may offer abhishek, Nilkanth Vatika, themed gardens and an evening Sat-Chit-Anand water show. The visitor page lists the complex as closed on Mondays.

description: The Swaminarayan Mandir at Vadtal, in Kheda district, Gujarat, is described by its own site as the headquarters of the Laxmi Narayan Dev Gadi; Wikipedia describes this as one of the two administrative seats of the Swaminarayan Sampraday, the other being at Ahmedabad. The central shrine is for Laxminarayan Dev, with Radha Krishna, Harikrishna Maharaj and other deities in side shrines. The temple is built on a lotus-shaped plinth and has nine domes. The complex includes a dharamshala and Gnyanbaug garden, and the site offers live darshan and daily darshan updates.

description: Shree Swaminarayan Mandir Kalupur stands in the old city of Ahmedabad, Gujarat, and is presented by its own site as the first temple of the Swaminarayan Sampraday built according to scriptural norms. According to Wikipedia, Swaminarayan assigned Anandanand Swami to oversee its construction, the land for it was granted by British officials (the Ahmedabad collector, Dunlop, relayed the approval), and it was inaugurated on 24 February 1822. Nar Narayan is enshrined at the centre, with Radha Krishna and other deities beside. The building is noted for Burma teak carving, a sabha mandap on sixty pillars and a mansion added in 1871. According to Wikipedia, it is the headquarters of the Nar Narayan Dev Gadi, one of the two administrative seats of the Sampraday; the Vadtal temple is the headquarters of the other.

description: Shri Swaminarayan Mandir at Gadhada (also called Gadhpur), in Gujarat, is known as Gopinathji Dev Mandir and is dedicated to Radha Krishna. Wikipedia describes a two-storey building with three domes on a high plinth, with halls, dharamshalas and kitchens, and reports that the spires were gold-plated in 2012.

description: At Sarangpur (also spelled Salangpur) in Gujarat's Botad area stands a Hanuman shrine where the deity is worshipped as Kashtabhanjan Dev, the remover of sorrows. Devotees believe the image drives away evil spirits, and Saturdays are set aside for a healing ritual for people troubled by mental illness or similar afflictions. description: The Talaja Caves are a group of rock-cut caves on the hills at Talaja in Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, near the Shetrunji river. They are a Buddhist monastic site; according to Wikipedia, the group has about 30 excavations, roughly half of them water tanks, and the chaitya and cells are dated there to the 2nd century BC, with Jain emblems later added to some cells and halls. The best-known feature is the Ebhal Mandapa, a large hall with octagonal pillars, and the facades carry chaitya-window motifs. Gujarat Tourism says the caves are about 2,000 years old and lie a short walk uphill; the same hill also holds a Jain temple and the Khodiyar Mata temple, so several traditions share the site. Dating is debated, and some historians treat it as uncertain.

description: The Uparkot Caves are a Buddhist rock-cut monastic complex inside the old Uparkot fort area of Junagadh, Gujarat, near the Adi Kadi step-well, and form part of the Junagadh Buddhist Cave Groups. Wikipedia assigns them to the 2nd to 3rd century AD, though one caption in the article gives a different date, so the dating should be treated as approximate. Wikipedia lists an assembly hall and a meditation cell among its features. The site appears in ASI's list of ticketed monuments.

description: Caves 30 to 34 form the Jain group of the Ellora rock-cut complex near Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar), Maharashtra, a World Heritage Site looked after by the Archaeological Survey of India. According to the ASI Aurangabad Circle, the group probably began around 800 CE and continued into the 11th century, and unlike most Ellora caves it faces south. Cave 30 is known as Chhota Kailas. Cave 32, the Indra Sabha, has a monolithic elephant in its courtyard facing a tall Manastambha pillar. Caves 32 and 33 (Jagannath Sabha) are linked by a first-floor passage, and the ASI says both retain notable later-period murals. Government tourism text notes the Jain caves hold the most surviving ceiling paintings at Ellora.

description: The Global Vipassana Pagoda is a meditation monument at Gorai, Borivali West, Mumbai, on a peninsula between Gorai creek and the Arabian Sea. According to Wikipedia, it was built entirely from voluntary donations in Burmese style, modelled on the Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon, as thanks to Myanmar and to Sayagyi U Ba Khin for preserving Vipassana, which S. N. Goenka taught in a non-sectarian form. Its central stone dome has no supporting pillars, and the hall is said to seat more than 8,000 meditators. Relics of the Buddha are enshrined in the dome, and the monument was inaugurated in February 2009. The adjoining Dhamma Pattana centre holds ten-day Vipassana courses, offered free of charge, and the complex includes a museum on the Buddha's life.

description: Karla (Karli) lies about 11 km from Lonavala in Maharashtra and holds a group of Buddhist rock-cut shrines and monasteries. According to Wikipedia, they were developed over several centuries, from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE, with donations from local merchants, monks, nuns and rulers supporting the community. The centrepiece is the Great Chaitya hall (Cave 8), which Wikipedia calls the largest and best preserved of its period, notable for its scale and its carved pillars and figures. The caves are a protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India. Beside the caves stands the temple of Goddess Ekvira (Ekveera), worshipped especially by the Agri and Koli communities of Mumbai. Local tradition holds that the Pandavas built the temple in a single night during their exile; this is a legend, not a documented history. The temple is a separate, living place of worship.

description: The Mahakali Caves, also called the Kondivite or Kondivita Caves, are a Buddhist rock-cut monastery in Andheri East, Mumbai, on a hill near the SEEPZ area. Wikipedia counts 19 caves in two groups, four to the north-west and fifteen to the south-east, carved in black basalt. Most are viharas, or monks' cells; the largest, Cave 9, is a chaitya hall with a stupa and several badly mutilated Buddha figures. Wikipedia places the excavation between the 4th century BCE and the 6th century CE, while the Incredible India page gives the 1st century BCE to the 6th century CE, so the dating is uncertain and the individual caves are dated differently. The site is a Buddhist monastery complex rather than a place of Hindu worship.

description: The Mandapeshwar Caves, are a rock-cut Shiva shrine near Mount Poinsur in Borivali, Mumbai. According to Wikipedia, Buddhist monks first carved the caves as viharas and Brahmins later occupied them as a Shaivite shrine. The cave has a sanctum, an antechamber, a pillared hall and an open forecourt, with lion-flanked steps. Sculptures include Nataraja, Lakulisa, Sadashiva and Ardhanarishvara, and a panel of the wedding of Shiva and Parvati is visible through a square window. Wikipedia says the ruins of a Portuguese church from 1544 stand above the cave. It also says most carvings are now damaged. Sources disagree on its age, with estimates ranging from about the 4th to 6th century to the 8th century, and the site is described as an archaeological heritage site protected under law.

description: The Nasik Caves, known locally as Pandavleni or the Trirashmi caves, are a group of about twenty-four rock-cut caves on the Trirashmi hill roughly 8 km south of Nashik city. description: Omkareshwar is a Shiva temple on the bank of the Mutha river in Shaniwar Peth, in the old part of Pune. According to the Pune Heritage site, Krishnajipant Chitrav built it between 1740 and 1760, in the Peshwa period, and Wikipedia's Shaniwar Peth article also lists it among the historic temples there. The east-facing complex has a gateway with a nagarkhana (drum house), a courtyard ringed by small rooms and a Nandi shrine before the main hall. The sanctum holds a large Shivalinga, and the roof is described as having nine domes and nine spires. Other shrines include Vishnu, Bhavani, Ganesh, Hanuman and Shani. The ghat nearby served as a cremation ground, and Mahashivaratri and Shravani Somvar are the main festivals.

description: Parvati Hill is a hillock in Pune, Maharashtra, and after Vetal Hill the second-highest point in the city, at about 640 m above sea level. Its summit holds a complex of temples to Shiva as Devdeveshwar, Vitthal and Rukmini, Vishnu, Kartikeya, Surya and Bhawani. A Peshwa-era museum displays weapons, coins and household objects, and the Peshwa's memorial stands on the hill. Visitors climb a flight of stone steps to reach the shrines.

description: Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Abchalnagar Sahib is a gurdwara in Nanded, Maharashtra, on the bank of the Godavari, and one of the five Takhts of the Sikhs. description: The Kolvi Caves lie near Kolvi village in Jhalawar district, southeastern Rajasthan, cut into a laterite hill. They are a Buddhist rock-cut site, not a Hindu temple. Wikipedia counts about fifty caves and reports that, of 64 monk cells once recorded, the Archaeological Survey of India has verified 45 similar structures. The site includes stupas and chaitya halls with Buddha figures in meditation and standing poses, some with circumambulation paths, and a standing Buddha about twelve feet tall showing the dharmachakra gesture. Wikipedia, citing Cunningham's observations, places the site at about 700 to 900 CE, with the style roughly 8th to 9th century CE,, later than the Bagh and Dhamnar caves, and describes a predominantly Mahayana character. Many figures are weathered, with their faces lost to natural decay.

description: Sanghiji is a Digambar Jain temple in Sanganer, about 16 km from Jaipur, Rajasthan, and a noted pilgrimage site of the tradition. According to Wikipedia, its principal deity is Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), the first Tirthankara, and the idol is traditionally described as extremely ancient. The red-stone temple follows the Nagara style with Maru-Gurjara touches such as carved pillars, bracket figures and lotus ceilings, and has a decorated double-storey entrance and several shikharas. Wikipedia cites a torana inscription dated V.S. 1011 for the final building phase. Its underground levels are said to be kept closed to visitors, and a 1999 account reports that a Jain monk, Muni Sudhasagar, brought out a number of idols from the temple. The shrine is managed by the Shri Digamber Jain Atishaya Kshetra Mandir committee.

description: The Sitaleshwar Temple is a Shiva temple at Jhalrapatan in Jhalawar district, Rajasthan, and belongs to the Chandrabhaga group of temples on the town's edge. According to Wikipedia, the sanctum holds a Shiva lingam with a Nandi facing it in the hall, and the temple was built in the 7th century with its pillared hall added in the 10th. It faces east and has a hall, an antechamber and a square sanctum. The original tower collapsed, leaving a flat roof with a small dome. The pillars are carved with female figures, directional guardians and ascetics, and the sanctum doorway shows Ganga and Yamuna and Lakulisa in the lintel. It is listed as a Monument of National Importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.
